g12-geography-ug5-t1.overview: Poverty is not one condition but several, and its causes run deep in both economic structures and human behaviour. This lesson distinguishes absolute, relative and persistent poverty, examines the causes of poverty and links violent conflict with chronic poverty.
objectives: Distinguish absolute, relative and persistent poverty using the textbook definitions
Identify the dimensions and indicators used to measure poverty, such as income, education and health care
Compare the structural and the behavioural or cultural explanations of poverty
Classify household resources into the five kinds of assets that determine poverty
Explain the three hypotheses that link violent conflict and poverty
g12-geography-ug5-t1.simple: Poverty is a deficiency of the basic needs a person, household or community needs to reach a basic standard of living. Absolute poverty means household income is below a level that makes meeting basic needs like food, shelter, safe water, education and health care impossible. Relative poverty means a household receives about 50 percent less than the average income, so it survives but cannot afford anything above the basics. Persistent poverty is long-term poverty, present in two of every three years. Poverty has structural causes, such as discrimination and low wages, and cultural causes, such as attitudes passed down in families. Poverty and violent conflict feed each other: conflict destroys economies and creates poverty, and poverty can help trigger conflict.
g12-geography-ug5-t1.detailed:
What poverty means. Poverty is generally considered a measure of deficiency of the basic needs that a person, household or community requires to meet a basic standard of living. The deficiency is measured as a lack of resources such as income and assets, or of capabilities such as skills, knowledge and technology. In 2015, approximately 10 percent of the world's population, 736 million people, lived in extreme poverty with incomes of less than $1.90 per day, and in 2017, 821 million people were malnourished. Such facts show why there is an urgent need for economic development to lift people out of poverty.

Absolute poverty. Absolute poverty is when household income is below a certain level, which makes it impossible for the person or family to meet the basic needs of life, including food, shelter, safe drinking water, education and health care. In this state, even if the country is growing economically, growth has no effect on people living below the poverty line. Absolute poverty compares households against a set income level, and this level varies from country to country depending on overall economic conditions.

Relative and persistent poverty. Relative poverty is when households receive 50 percent less than average household incomes, so they have some money but not enough to afford anything above basic needs. It is sometimes called a relative deficiency, because these people are not in total poverty yet do not enjoy the same standard of living as everyone else, whether in internet access, clean clothes, a safe home or education. Relative poverty can also become permanent, trapping families in a low relative income box. When the relative approach is used, there is also persistent poverty: households receive 50 or 60 percent less income than average incomes every 2 out of 3 years, and its long-term consequences are the most damaging for the economy and society.

Measuring poverty. The textbook's selected dimensions and indicators show how poverty is assessed: income (net income per capita), education (child school attendance and adult illiteracy), health care (health service, health status and health insurance), access to social services (electricity, drinking water, toilet, cooking fuel, transportation and housing), and social security (work status, pension insurance, consumer durables and social insurance). The summary of the unit also identifies four primary elements of poverty: economic, cognitive, normative and power politics.

Structural causes. The structural approach points to systemic reasons for poverty: racial and gender discrimination embedded in markets and institutions, the profit motive and consequent low wages that make it difficult for families to escape poverty, and failure to invest sufficiently in education, health care and social insurance. These factors reduce opportunity and increase economic insecurity. Structural approaches point to patriarchy, capitalism, white privilege and racism as fundamental causes of most poverty in Western economies, and are typically favoured by those on the political left.

Behavioural or cultural causes, and poverty as people describe it. Other researchers emphasise culture, behaviour and personal differences: a poverty culture, a set of attitudes such as fatalism and the rejection of hard work and rationality, passed from parents to children, which perpetuates bad, self-defeating decisions and hence poverty. This view insists each person has free will and is ultimately responsible for their own life, and is typically favoured by conservatives and libertarians. Poor people themselves emphasise lack of income and assets for basic necessities, a sense of voicelessness and powerlessness in state and social institutions, and vulnerability to adverse shocks linked to an inability to cope with them.

Conflict and poverty. Violent conflict and poverty are inter-linked. Three hypotheses describe the relationship. First, conflict causes poverty: battlefield deaths, disablement and displacement raise dependency ratios, while macro-economic effects include falls in GDP per capita, food production, exports, gross investment, government revenue and expenditure; war can lead to entitlement collapse and famine, and protracted collapsed-state conflicts lead to intergenerational exclusion and chronic poverty. Second, poverty causes conflict: conflicts are multi-causal, so poverty may act as a permissive factor, a structural cause, a trigger or an accelerator rather than a deterministic link. Third, resource wealth causes conflict: World Bank research argues rebellion is motivated by greed, since war cannot be fought on hopes and hatreds; civil wars occur when rebel organisations are financially viable, so the feasibility of predation determines the risk of conflict.

workedExamples.problem: A household in Addis Ababa earns 40 percent of the average household income. Its members eat but cannot afford electricity or internet, unlike their neighbours. Classify their poverty.
workedExamples.given: Income is about 50 percent below the average household income; basic food is obtained but conditions above the basics are out of reach.
workedExamples.formula: Absolute poverty means basic needs cannot be met; relative poverty means income is 50 percent less than the average.
workedExamples.substitution: The family is not in total poverty but receives roughly half the average income.
workedExamples.calculation: The condition matches the definition of relative poverty, and since it repeats year after year it may become permanent relative poverty.
workedExamples.answer: Relative poverty, at risk of becoming permanent relative poverty.

workedExamples.problem: A family's income was below 60 percent of the national average in two of the last three years. Which poverty concept applies and why is it important?
workedExamples.given: Income fell 50 to 60 percent below average in 2 of 3 years.
workedExamples.formula: Persistent poverty: households receive 50 or 60 percent less than average incomes every 2 out of 3 years.
workedExamples.substitution: The family's record fits the definition exactly.
workedExamples.calculation: Long-term poverty has more impactful consequences on economic and social conditions than short spells, so this concept matters most.
workedExamples.answer: Persistent poverty; it shows chronic disadvantage rather than a temporary fall.

workedExamples.problem: A rural Ethiopian household has a plot of land, family labour and good health, an ox-drawn plough, small savings and credit from an iqub, and membership of an iddir network. Sort these into the five asset kinds.
workedExamples.given: Land, labour, skills and health; access to infrastructure; savings and credit; networks of contacts and reciprocal obligations.
workedExamples.formula: Assets: human, natural, physical, financial, social.
workedExamples.substitution: Labour, skills and health are human assets; land is natural; the plough and infrastructure access are physical; savings, credit and iqub are financial; the iddir network and social influence are social.
workedExamples.calculation: Each item maps onto one asset class, and poverty analysis asks about the assets, the returns to them and the volatility of those returns.
workedExamples.answer: Human: labour, skills, health; Natural: land; Physical: plough and infrastructure; Financial: savings, credit, iqub; Social: iddir membership and influence.

workedExamples.problem: A conflict-affected country is compared with a peaceful neighbour of similar size. Using the textbook, predict which macro-economic indicators fell in the conflict country.
workedExamples.given: The country has experienced prolonged violent conflict.
workedExamples.formula: Known macro-economic effects of conflict on affected countries.
workedExamples.substitution: GDP per capita, food production, exports, gross investment, and government revenue and expenditure all decline.
workedExamples.calculation: Higher dependency ratios from deaths, disablement and displacement add to the economic damage, and entitlement collapse can produce famine.
workedExamples.answer: Conflict country: falls in GDP per capita, food production, exports, gross investment and government revenue and expenditure, plus famine risk.

commonMistakes: Believing economic growth automatically removes absolute poverty; growth does not help those below the poverty line.
Treating relative poverty as total poverty; the relatively poor have some money, just not enough above basic needs.
Confusing persistent poverty with a one-year drop in income; it must recur in 2 out of 3 years.
Assuming poverty has a single cause; it is caused by labor market issues, education, demographics, race, policies and culture.
Thinking conflict only creates poverty; poverty can also be a permissive or causal factor behind conflict.
Believing all conflict is driven by grievance; World Bank research stresses greed and the feasibility of predation.
applications: Counting households below the $1.90 per day line when estimating extreme poverty in a woreda like the textbook's global 736 million estimate of 2015.
Using the dimension-indicator table to assess school attendance, drinking water and electricity access in your own kebele.
Explaining famine risk after war by connecting displacement, dependency ratios and entitlement collapse.
Discussing how Ethiopia's safety-net and education investments respond to the structural view of poverty.
Analysing how mineral resource wealth may raise conflict risk where rebel groups can be financially viable.
g12-geography-ug5-t1.summary: Poverty has many faces: absolute poverty denies basic needs, relative poverty leaves households at about half the average income, and persistent poverty repeats this 2 out of every 3 years. Its causes combine structural factors such as discrimination, low wages and under-investment with cultural factors such as fatalism passed between generations. Conflict and poverty reinforce each other through falling output, investment and revenue, entitlement collapse and famine, while greed over financially viable resources can drive conflict.

g12-geography-ug5-t2.overview: Globalization links the world through trade, finance, media and culture, bringing both gains and losses. This lesson defines globalization and weighs its advantages and limitations for developing countries like Ethiopia.
objectives: Define globalization and describe its acceleration over the last half century
Identify the three fields in which globalization affects developing countries
Explain the advantages of globalization for Global North and Global South
Evaluate the disadvantages of globalization, including environmental and cultural costs
Assess the impact of globalization on developing countries using Ethiopia as an example
g12-geography-ug5-t2.simple: Globalization is the process through which the world becomes more linked as a result of greater commerce and cultural interaction. It has happened for hundreds of years but accelerated dramatically in the last half century, as the biggest companies became multinational corporations with subsidiaries in many countries. For developing countries it works through three fields: economic and trade processes, education and health systems, and culture. Its benefits include increased free trade, easier transport, mass media sharing information, spread of democratic ideals and reduced likelihood of war between developed nations. Its drawbacks include pollution by corporations escaping weak regulation, cheap-labour exploitation, brain drain of skilled workers, loss of cultural diversity and the risk of economic disruption spreading worldwide.
g12-geography-ug5-t2.detailed:
The basic concept. Globalization has become one of the world's most contentious issues. The most common definition is the process through which the world becomes more linked as a result of greater commerce and cultural interaction. It has increased the production of goods and services, and the biggest companies are no longer national firms but multinational corporations with subsidiaries in many countries. Globalization has been happening for hundreds of years but has accelerated dramatically in the last half century, and the term now describes the trend of countries joining together economically, through politics and education, seeing themselves as part of the world as a whole.

Economic and trade processes. Globalization helps developing countries deal with the rest of the world to increase economic growth and solve poverty problems. In the past, developing countries could not tap the world economy because of trade barriers. With globalization, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund encouraged developing countries to undertake market reforms through large loans, so many opened their markets by removing tariffs, and developed countries invested in them, creating jobs. Rapid growth in India and China caused world poverty to decrease, yet Africa still has the highest poverty rates, and rural China, which does not tap global markets, suffers greatly. Developed countries also set up companies in developing nations to exploit low wages, causing pollution in countries with poor regulation, while relocations can increase unemployment in the developed countries themselves.

Education, health and brain drain. Globalization contributed to developing health and education systems: demand for jobs requiring higher skills pushed people to gain higher education, and economic gains raised living standards, life expectancy and spending on health, so illiteracy rates fell in many developing countries. An important drawback is that globalized competition pushes highly educated and qualified professionals, such as scientists, doctors, engineers and IT specialists, to migrate to developed countries for higher wages, decreasing skilled labour in the developing countries.

Culture effects. Globalization changed cultural traits enormously as people imitate cultures like America and European countries. Extreme dependence on globalization may destroy local cultures, traditions, identities, customs and even languages; it was witnessed in some Arab countries (Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan) that cultures were negatively affected, clothing and behaviour totally changed, and many local words disappeared as English and French words spread. Family life also changed: young people increasingly leave their families to live alone at age 18, the extended family grows smaller, and such changes are observed in many urban areas of Ethiopia.

Advantages of globalization. Globalization increases free trade between countries; increased capital liquidity allows investors in developed nations to invest in developing countries, and corporations gain flexibility to operate across borders. Global mass media ties the world together and allows vital information to be shared worldwide. Joining together economically reduces and can eradicate cultural barriers, increasing the global village effect; globalization spread democratic ideals and greater independence to developing countries in the Global South. Reduction of the likelihood of war between well developed nations is probably one of the primary benefits, and environmental protection efforts in developed nations increase.

Disadvantages of globalization. Globalization can decrease environmental integrity as polluting corporations take advantage of weak regulatory rules in developing nations. The hunt for cheap labour creates jobs but deepens inequality between developed and developing countries. Mass media controlled by huge corporations limits cultural diversity and free expression. Other listed disadvantages include the chance that economic disruption in one nation affects all nations, corporate influence exceeding that of civil society and individuals, violent reactions to protect cultural heritage, greater risk of diseases being transported unintentionally between nations, spread of a materialistic lifestyle that sees consumption as the path to prosperity, international bodies such as the World Trade Organization infringing on national and individual sovereignty, and increased chances of civil war within and between developing countries vying for resources. Globalization is here to stay, so nations of the Global North and Global South must work together to spread its benefits and reduce its risks.

workedExamples.calculation: Integration brings investment and jobs; exclusion keeps poverty high, so the difference follows from market integration.
workedExamples.answer: Regions that integrated into the global economy grew and cut poverty; those that did not, including rural China and most of Africa, stayed poor.

workedExamples.substitution: Tariffs and reform loans are trade; higher education demand and falling illiteracy are education and health; dress and language imitation are cultural.

commonMistakes: Thinking globalization is only recent; it has been happening for hundreds of years, though it accelerated dramatically in the last half century.
Believing globalization benefits everyone equally; basically the developed world has benefited most, as it can sell more goods to the global South.
Assuming foreign investment is always harmless; factories set up for low wages can cause pollution in poorly regulated countries.
Forgetting that relocation of industries can increase unemployment in the developed countries themselves.
Thinking mass media control only affects entertainment; it also limits cultural diversity and free expression.
Believing globalization means homogeneity only; its effect can also provoke violent reactions to preserve cultural heritage.
applications: Tracing a foreign-owned garment factory in Ethiopia's industrial parks as an example of investment drawn by low wages.
Discussing how Ethiopian nurses and IT specialists migrating abroad illustrate brain drain.
Comparing how Ethiopian coffee exports reach global markets once trade barriers fall versus before market opening.
Assessing local TV and internet content to see whether mass media spreads cultural heritage or dilutes it.
Debating whether Ethiopia benefits more from joining global markets or from protecting its infant industries, as the North-South division suggests.
g12-geography-ug5-t2.summary: Globalization is the process by which growing commerce and cultural interaction link the world, now dominated by multinational corporations and accelerated over the last half century. It brings free trade, investment, information flows, cultural exchange and reduced war between developed nations, but also pollution from weakly regulated factories, cheap-labour inequality, brain drain, cultural loss and risk of global economic disruption. Developing countries in the Global South gain most when they integrate into world markets and manage its cultural and environmental risks.

g12-geography-ug5-t3.overview: Why do some regions and countries grow richer while others fall behind? This lesson explains the convergence and divergence hypotheses, the causes and effects of trade imbalance, and how inequality is measured, including the Gini coefficient.
objectives: Explain the concept of economic inequality between regions and countries
Describe the three arguments supporting the convergence or catching-up hypothesis
Explain divergence and why inequality widened in some economies
Analyse the causes and effects of trade imbalance between countries
Evaluate regional and country inequality using per capita GDP and the Gini coefficient
g12-geography-ug5-t3.simple: Economic inequality between regions and countries is both a simple and a very complex idea. The convergence, or catching-up, hypothesis expects less developed countries to grow faster than more developed ones, because latecomers can adopt existing technologies, enjoy low wages and shifting labour from farm to industry. However, widening income inequality is the defining challenge of our time: skill premiums and financial deepening have raised inequality. An important indicator is the trade balance: a trade imbalance occurs when the cost of a country's imports exceeds its exports, calculated as imports minus exports. Inequality is most often measured with per capita GDP and the Gini coefficient, where 0 means perfect equality and 1 means maximal inequality. Sub-Saharan Africa shows among the greatest inequality in the world.
g12-geography-ug5-t3.detailed:
A simple yet complex idea. Inequality has moved people like hardly any other concept, yet it is a very complex notion studied by philosophers, statisticians, political theorists, sociologists and economists. From the ancient period to the present, theories have seen trade as a key instrument in determining the trend of regional and country economic inequality, taken into account by the convergence and divergence hypotheses with their distinct assumptions.

The convergence hypothesis. The catching-up hypothesis states that less developed countries and regions should be expected to grow faster than more developed ones, so inter-country inequality should decline over time. Three main arguments support it. First, latecomers into the world of modern economic growth enjoy an advantage because they can simply adopt and exploit technologies the pioneers had to develop themselves. Second, diminishing returns to factor inputs imply less developed economies have low production costs from low wages, so for equivalent rates of investment they should achieve higher growth. Third, shifting large amounts of labour from farm to industry boosts general labour productivity, though this source of growth declines as development proceeds.

Divergence instead. Nevertheless, widening income inequality is the defining challenge of our time: in advanced economies the gap between rich and poor is at its highest level in decades. Evidence for divergence includes technological development and the associated rise in skill, together with the collapse of various labour market institutions in advanced and developing countries, and growing skill premiums tied to expanding inequality in advanced nations while financial deepening accompanies rising inequality in developing countries.

Trade imbalance and how it is calculated. An important indicator of regional and national inequality is the trade balance. A trade imbalance occurs when the cost of a country's imports exceeds the cost of its exports, also called a negative trade balance; a trade deficit may be calculated by subtracting the total value of exports from the total value of imports. Causes: a country does not produce what it requires and must borrow from other countries to pay for imports, a current account deficit; deficits also arise when companies manufacture goods abroad, so raw materials count as exports while finished goods count as imports. Effects: a deficit can enhance living standards through a broader range of cheaper goods and can reduce inflation threats, but over time it may outsource more jobs, as the home country creates fewer jobs in certain industries while foreign companies hire workers to meet export demand.

Measuring inequality. Economic inequality measures the disparity between the percentage of population and the percentage of resources, such as income, received by that population. The most often used metric for global economic disparity is per capita GDP, assessed against physical attributes (natural ability is unequally distributed), personal preferences (relative valuation of leisure and work differs), social processes (pressure to work varies across fields) and public policy (tax, labour and education policies shape distribution). It was long believed inequality in Africa was modest because most people were generally impoverished, until it was found that inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa is among the greatest in the world, in both income and non-income circumstances.

The widening global imbalance. Gini coefficients of gross and net incomes have increased substantially since 1990 in most of the developed world; inequality has remained stable on average in developing countries, but at a much higher level than in advanced economies. Asia and Eastern Europe saw marked increases, while Latin America recorded notable declines yet remains the most unequal region in the world. Income inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa is one of the most unequal despite low per capita income; non-income inequalities, particularly between men and women and between regions, persist over time, and asset-based and capability-based inequalities tend to be higher in rural than urban areas. Where initial income differences are significant, growth is less effective at alleviating poverty, so economic expansion and inequality reduction must go hand in hand. During 1990-2012, market income inequality in advanced economies increased by an average of 50 Gini points compared with a 3 Gini point increase in the net Gini coefficient. A Gini coefficient of 0 reflects perfect equality, where all income values are the same, while a coefficient of 1 (or 100 percent) reflects maximal inequality.

The growing extra pay for skilled work, associated with expanding income inequality in advanced nations.

workedExamples.problem: Country A records a Gini coefficient of 0.31 and Country B records 0.63. Interpreting the values, which country is more unequal and what would 0 and 1 mean?
workedExamples.given: Gini A = 0.31; Gini B = 0.63; scale 0 to 1.
workedExamples.formula: Gini 0 = perfect equality; Gini 1 (or 100 percent) = maximal inequality.
workedExamples.substitution: 0.63 is much closer to 1 than 0.31 is.
workedExamples.calculation: The higher coefficient indicates a wider gap between income shares, so B is more unequal.
workedExamples.answer: Country B is more unequal; 0 means all incomes are equal and 1 means maximal inequality. B resembles the high-inequality level cited for Sub-Saharan Africa.

workedExamples.problem: A latecomer country can adopt existing technologies, pays low wages and is shifting labour from farms to industry. Which hypothesis predicts faster growth for it, and which three arguments apply?

workedExamples.substitution: Latecomers exploit technologies pioneers developed; low wages give cost advantage per diminishing returns; farm-to-industry shift boosts productivity.
workedExamples.calculation: All three conditions match the stated arguments, so convergence is predicted.
workedExamples.answer: The convergence hypothesis, supported by all three arguments: technology adoption, diminishing returns with low wages, and the farm-to-industry productivity shift.

workedExamples.problem: A country produces almost nothing it requires and finances imports by borrowing, and local firms also produce goods abroad that are shipped back home. Identify the two causes of trade imbalance shown and one long-term effect.
workedExamples.given: Borrowing to pay for imports; off-shore manufacturing of finished goods.
workedExamples.formula: Causes of trade imbalance from the textbook.
workedExamples.substitution: Borrowing for imports is a current account deficit; raw materials shipped out count as exports while finished goods ship back as imports.
workedExamples.calculation: Over time importing more than is bought domestically can shift jobs to foreign countries as foreign firms hire for export demand.
workedExamples.answer: Current account deficit (borrowing to import) and off-shoring of manufacturing; long-term effect: job outsourcing to foreign countries.

commonMistakes: Assuming trade always reduces inequality; despite theory, trade is increasing inequality between the global north and south.
Confusing a trade deficit with positive growth; a deficit means imports exceed exports in money value.
Believing the Gini coefficient has no limits; scores must be interpreted together with the scale of 0 (equality) to 1 (maximal inequality).
Thinking Africa's low average income means low inequality; Sub-Saharan Africa has among the greatest inequality in the world.
Assuming inequality is only an urban problem; asset-based and capability-based inequalities tend to be higher in rural areas.
Forgetting that economic expansion and inequality reduction must go hand in hand to significantly cut poverty.

g12-geography-ug5-t3.summary: Inequality between regions and countries is judged through the convergence hypothesis, which expects latecomers with adopted technology, low wages and farm-to-industry labour shifts to catch up, against divergence evidence from rising skill premiums and financial deepening. Trade imbalance, calculated as imports minus exports, signals inequality when a country borrows to finance imports, and it can cut local jobs over time even though it lowers prices. Per capita GDP and the Gini coefficient measure disparity, with Sub-Saharan Africa among the most unequal regions despite low income levels.

g12-geography-ug5-t4.overview: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain, and it varies sharply across the world map. This lesson examines the types of corruption, the geography of the Corruption Perceptions Index, its causes, its economic consequences, and remedial measures.
objectives: Define corruption and explain why it has no single universal definition
Distinguish bribery, theft of public assets and patronage as the three broad categories
Differentiate petty and grand corruption, and define kleptocracy, crony capitalism and kick-backs
Interpret Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index scores and world distribution
Explain the economic effects of corruption and the measures recommended to fight it
g12-geography-ug5-t4.simple: Corruption is most commonly defined as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. It is simultaneously a political, economic, legal and moral phenomenon, and no single definition fits every circumstance because it takes petty, large-scale, systemic, occasional, implicit and explicit forms. Its three broad categories are bribery, theft of public assets and patronage (favoritism). Low-value transactions are petty corruption, large-value ones grand corruption, and combinations produce kleptocracy and crony capitalism. Because corruption is hidden, geographers rely on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, scored 0 (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt) since 1995. Corruption is most characteristic of low-income, closed economies with little media freedom and education, and it damages investment, public spending, taxes and talent allocation.
g12-geography-ug5-t4.detailed:
The concept. Critical geography examines corruption as an objective collection of deviant actions predominantly affecting states, particularly in the Global South, and shows how corruption explanations get politicised and linked with material and geographical power regimes; urban informality is a significant linked issue in both the North and South. The term covers a wide range of behaviours differing in cause and effect across space and time: corruption can be petty or large-scale, systemic or occasional, implicit or explicit, committed by individuals, so there is no single definition applicable to all circumstances. It is commonly defined as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain, and as evil and a disastrous personal failing; legally, however, judicial systems punish acts, not character. Corruption is simultaneously a political, economic, legal and moral phenomenon. Many studies show it correlates negatively with economic growth even after controlling for institutional efficiency, and it creates uncertainty for investors and raises investment risk.

Types of corruption. Three broad categories of human action are distinguished. Bribery, the most familiar, is payments by individuals or firms to public officials to influence administrative decisions covering the wide scope of government regulation. Theft of public assets occurs as unilateral embezzlement by officials or through collusion between officials and private agents, including illegal transfer of real or financial assets at below-market prices, tax evasion and diversion of public funds into private pockets. Patronage, sometimes called favoritism, nepotism or clienteles, is the preferential treatment of firms or individuals over government contracts or transfer payments, exchanged for special favors such as financial rewards or professional opportunities. Corruption acts are also characterised by transaction value: low value is petty and large value is grand corruption; typically the larger the transaction, the higher the position of the officials involved. Combinations produce specific types: systematic theft at a grand scale by high officials is kleptocracy; systematic patronage with large stakes is crony capitalism or government capture; and kick-backs describe bribery that involves theft of public assets or patronage.

The geography of corruption. Corruption has a geographical essence because social processes are distributed unevenly across space: its causes, nature and consequences differ from place to place depending on historical, cultural, legal and political organization. Its incidence is hard to establish empirically because its committers are adept at keeping it hidden, so analyses rely on Transparency International, a global nongovernmental organisation that monitors and combats corruption, measures it, exposes cases, advises companies and develops tools. Since 1995 it issues the annual Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI), a composite indicator based on surveys and expert assessments by 13 sources, with at least three sources per country, scored 0 (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt).

The world distribution. Only a small group, including Canada, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand, has CPI numbers of 80 or higher, about 1.7 percent of the world's population (118.6 million). A secondary tier of scores 60-79 includes several European countries, the United States, Japan, Botswana, Israel, Taiwan and the United Arab Emirates, about one-eighth of humanity. Moderately corrupt governments, scores 40-59, include European, African, Middle Eastern and a few Asian states such as South Korea. By far the largest group, almost three-fourths of humanity, consists of 82 states with scores of 20-39 holding more than 5.2 billion people; corruption is the norm in most societies by this measure. Finally 14 states score below 20, extremely corrupt, including failed states such as Somalia, Afghanistan and Yemen, and others marked by extreme poverty (Haiti), war (Iraq) and totalitarian government (Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, North Korea). Regionally, the worst offenders lie in Africa and the Middle East; the second-most corrupt group covers much of East, South and Southeast Asia (except Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Malaysia), most of Africa and Spanish-speaking Latin America; the third group (40-59) includes Brazil, South Africa, Turkey and Saudi Arabia; the fourth (60-79) includes the United States, Japan, most of Europe and notably Botswana, Africa's least-corrupt country. In the 2016 table, the tiers held 118.6, 854.4, 694.2, 5210.2 and 267.7 million people respectively.

Causes and consequences. Though corruption differs from country to country, the most corrupt countries characteristically are low-income countries, have closed economies, show visible religious influence, suffer low media freedom and have relatively low levels of education. Its serious impacts on public finances: corruption increases the volume of public investments at the expense of private investments, because high officials manipulate expenditure to get bribes; it redirects public expenditure from basic functioning and maintenance toward new equipment; it pulls money away from fixed assets needed for health and education where commissions are harder to get; it reduces the effectiveness of public investments and infrastructure; and it can reduce tax revenues by compromising the state's ability to collect taxes and fees. Its influence operates through impacts on investments, the allocation of talents, public spending and taxes.

Remedial measures. Suggested system-level remedies include leadership (top leaders must model honesty, integrity, hard work and political will for reform), credibility (investigation and punishment must reach even the leader's own group, convincing both demand and supply sides of corrupt deals that government is serious), involving people (publicity campaigns and cooperation of citizens, who have firsthand experience and can supply information), a responsible press to gather, analyse and disseminate information and build momentum for reform, oversight bodies (watchdogs that are useful in some instances but can be misused for political gain, even requiring a watchdog over the watchdog), and improving institutions such as the legal framework, smoother business procedures, more efficient police, a strengthened auditor general's office and a responsible inspector general empowered to investigate and prosecute corruption.

keyTerms.def: The abuse of entrusted power for private gain; simultaneously a political, economic, legal and moral phenomenon.
Payments by individuals or firms to public officials to influence administrative decisions under their responsibility.
Embezzlement by public officials or their collusion with private agents, including tax evasion and diversion of public funds.
Favoritism or nepotism: preferential treatment by public officials in allocating contracts or transfers, repaid with special favors.
The distinction by transaction value; typically the larger the corrupt transaction, the higher the officials' position.
Systematic theft at a grand scale by high public officials.
Systematic patronage with large stakes, also known as government capture.
Transparency International's annual composite index, issued since 1995, scored 0 (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt).

workedExamples.problem: A country receives a CPI score of 45 in Transparency International's index. Into which tier of corruption does it fall, and which group of states does the textbook place there?
workedExamples.given: CPI score = 45; scale runs 0 (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt).
workedExamples.formula: Tiers: 80 and above least corrupt; 60-79 slightly; 40-59 moderately; 20-39 very corrupt; below 20 extremely corrupt.

workedExamples.answer: Moderately corrupt (40-59), the tier shared by states such as South Korea, Brazil, South Africa, Turkey and Saudi Arabia.

workedExamples.substitution: (a) payment to influence an administrative decision; (b) diversion of public funds; (c) preferential treatment of relatives; (d) small-value bribery.
workedExamples.calculation: Each act matches a defined category, and value separates grand from petty.
workedExamples.answer: (a) bribery (grand, tied to a contract); (b) theft of public assets; (c) patronage; (d) petty bribery.

workedExamples.given: Very corrupt tier: 82 states, population 5210.2 million.
workedExamples.formula: Share of world population = tier population / total world population x 100.
workedExamples.calculation: 5210.2 / 7145.1 is about 0.729, that is about 72.9 percent, more than 5.2 billion people or almost three-fourths of humanity.
workedExamples.answer: 5210.2 million people, about 72.9 percent of the world's population.

workedExamples.problem: A ministry divides its budget: more goes to new equipment with large commissions, less to maintaining clinics and schools. Explain which documented effect of corruption this illustrates and how it reaches the wider economy.
workedExamples.given: Budget shifted from maintenance and health/education toward equipment.
workedExamples.formula: Documented effects of corruption on public finances and its transmission channels.
workedExamples.substitution: Corruption redirects the composition of public expenditure from basic functioning and maintenance toward new equipment, and pulls it away from fixed assets for health and education.
workedExamples.calculation: The influence then operates through public spending, investments and taxes, lowering the effectiveness of public investment and infrastructure.
workedExamples.answer: It illustrates expenditure redirection away from health and education; it spreads through the channels of public spending, investment, taxes and the allocation of talents.

commonMistakes: Assuming corruption has one universal definition; it can be petty or large-scale, systemic or occasional, implicit or explicit.
Thinking courts punish corrupt character; legally, judicial systems punish acts, not character.
Confusing patronage with bribery: patronage is preferential treatment repaid with special favors, not necessarily direct payment.
Reading a high CPI score as more corrupt; a score of 100 means least corrupt.
Believing corruption harms only government accounts; it also raises investor uncertainty and risk, lowering growth.
Assuming watchdog bodies always work; they can be misused for political gain, even needing a watchdog over the watchdog.
applications: Interpreting Ethiopia's position on the CPI map and discussing why incidence is hard to measure because committers hide it.
Visiting a local anti-corruption commission office to record its duties, common corruption types and investigation methods, as the textbook activity suggests.
Explaining how diverted road or health budgets reduce the effectiveness of public infrastructure in a woreda.
Debating whether publicity campaigns or institutional reform is more effective against corruption in Ethiopia's context.
Mapping the world tiers of corruption to see why the worst offenders cluster in Africa and the Middle East.
g12-geography-ug5-t4.summary: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain, taking bribery, theft of public assets and patronage forms, from petty low-value acts to grand-scale kleptocracy and crony capitalism. Because it is hidden, geographers rely on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, which since 1995 has shown most countries as moderately to severely corrupt, with very corrupt states holding nearly three-fourths of humanity. Corruption thrives with poverty, closed economies, weak media and education, and it damages investment, spending, taxes and talent, so remedies span leadership example, credibility, public involvement, a responsible press, oversight bodies and stronger institutions.

g12-geography-ug5-t5.overview: Health crises are global problems with sharply unequal local impacts. This lesson explores the global financing gap in health, the history of pandemics, and the current crises of HIV/AIDS, Ebola and COVID-19, including what happened in Ethiopia in 1918.
objectives: Describe the global context of health crises, including access and financing inequalities
Differentiate epidemic from pandemic and outline the history of pandemics
Explain the causes and impacts of malaria as a continuing African crisis
Compare the HIV/AIDS, Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks using dates, places and figures
Assess why poor countries suffer more from health crises than developed countries
g12-geography-ug5-t5.simple: Globally, about 2 billion people lack access to basic health services. Malaria infects more than 500 million people a year and kills more than a million, roughly one death every 30 seconds, hitting Africa hardest and costing the continent about $12 billion in lost productivity annually. Poor countries pay the highest out-of-pocket share for health, and only 12 percent of the $3.2 trillion spent worldwide on health in 2002 reached nations holding 90 percent of the illness burden. A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread beyond a country's borders; historical examples run from the Plague of Athens in 430 BC to the 1918 Spanish Flu with 50 million deaths. Current crises include HIV/AIDS (first identified 1981, 35 million deaths), Ebola (index case December 2013 in Guinea, 11,310 deaths in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone) and COVID-19 (declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020, more than 75 million cases and 1.6 million deaths by December 2020).
g12-geography-ug5-t5.detailed:
The global context. An estimated 2 billion individuals worldwide do not have access to basic health services, producing shocking levels of preventable illness. Residents of poor nations pay the highest proportion of their health-care costs out of pocket because their governments lack the financial resources for a functional, accessible system; an estimated 150 million people and 25 million households cannot pay for health care at all due to financial constraints. Only 12 percent of the $3.2 trillion spent on health care worldwide in 2002 was spent in low- and middle-income nations, which carry 90 percent of the world's illness burden. Health-sector aid did rise over 50 percent between 2002 and 2005, driven by donors such as the United States and new financing partnerships like the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization, yet funding remains significantly below estimated needs.

Malaria, the persistent burden. Malaria infects more than 500 million people a year and kills more than a million, equating to approximately one death from malaria every 30 seconds. Its greatest impact is in Africa, where it is the leading cause of mortality among children, and it costs the continent around $12 billion in lost productivity each year.

What a pandemic is and where it began. In infectious disease, a pandemic is the worst-case scenario: when an epidemic spreads beyond a country's borders, the disease officially becomes a pandemic. Communicable diseases existed among hunter-gatherers, but the shift to agrarian life 10,000 years ago created communities that made epidemics more possible; malaria, tuberculosis, leprosy, influenza and smallpox first appeared in that period. As city regions traded and fought each other, conditions for worldwide pandemics became more likely. The Great Plague of Athens in 430 BC, during the Peloponnesian War, is one key recorded pandemic: after passing through Libya, Ethiopia and Egypt it crossed the Athenian walls during the Spartan siege, as much as two-thirds of the population died, with fever, thirst, bloody throat and tongue, red skin and lesions; suspected typhoid fever weakened Athens and contributed to its defeat.

The 1918 Spanish Flu. Up to the 1918 pandemic, around 11 vastly accelerated pandemics were reported after Athens. The avian-borne Spanish flu, the most famous in history, caused 50 million deaths worldwide. It was first observed in Europe, the United States and parts of Asia before swiftly spreading around the world, with no effective drugs or vaccines. Wire-service reports of a flu outbreak in Madrid in the spring of 1918 gave the pandemic its name; by October, hundreds of thousands of Americans had died and body storage reached crisis levels. The threat disappeared in the summer of 1919 as most infected people either developed immunity or died. In Ethiopia this crisis is remembered as the 1918 Great Ethiopian Influenza, Ye Hedar Beshita, a historic epidemic tied to the same global Spanish Flu.

HIV/AIDS and Ebola today. First identified in 1981, AIDS weakens the immune system, leading to death from illnesses the body would normally combat; carriers are highly infectious through blood and genital fluid, and the disease destroys t-cells. AIDS was first observed in America. Treatments slow its progress, but 35 million people worldwide have died since its discovery and a cure is yet to be found. Ebola's index patient was reported in December 2013: an 18-month-old boy from a small village in Guinea, believed infected by bats. Ebola exposed what happens when a country lacks the minimum core capacity to detect, report and rapidly respond to outbreaks; the three most affected states, Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, had vulnerable public health infrastructures in the aftermath of civil war, with broken sanitation. The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern; 11,310 deaths were reported in the three countries, with an additional 36 cases and 15 deaths outside them.

COVID-19. On March 11, 2020 the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 virus a pandemic after it infected over 118,000 individuals in 114 nations in three months, and the spread was far from finished. Symptoms include respiratory problems, fever and cough, which can lead to pneumonia and death; it spreads through droplets from sneezes. The first reported case appeared November 17, 2019 in China's Hubei Province. Without a vaccine available, the virus spread beyond Chinese borders to nearly every country; by December 2020 it had infected more than 75 million people and caused more than 1.6 million deaths, with new cases growing faster than ever at more than 500,000 reported each day on average. Poor countries suffer most from such crises, because global inequalities and chronic poor governance limit their capacity to respond, even though health crises affect both poor and rich nations.

keyTerms.def: An outbreak of disease within a country or region; officially a pandemic once it spreads beyond a country's borders.
The worst-case scenario of infectious disease spread, crossing national boundaries across the world.
A mosquito-borne disease infecting over 500 million people yearly and killing more than a million, with its greatest impact in Africa.
A disease first identified in 1981 that weakens the immune system by destroying t-cells; 35 million people have died of it.
A viral disease whose index patient appeared in December 2013 in Guinea, spreading to Liberia and Sierra Leone with 11,310 reported deaths.
A respiratory disease first reported in Hubei Province, China, on November 17, 2019; declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020.
The proportion of health costs individuals pay themselves, highest for residents of poor nations.
The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, a financing partnership created as health aid rose after 2002.

workedExamples.given: Deaths in three countries = 11,310; deaths outside = 15.

workedExamples.problem: Malaria kills more than a million people a year. Using the statement that this equates to one death every 30 seconds, check the figure and state where mortality is highest and the economic cost.
workedExamples.given: More than 1 million deaths per year; one death every 30 seconds; Africa hardest hit.
workedExamples.formula: Deaths per 30-second interval = annual deaths / number of 30-second intervals in a year.
workedExamples.substitution: 1,000,000 / (365 x 24 x 120) = 1,000,000 / 1,051,200, which is almost exactly 1 per 30 seconds.
workedExamples.calculation: Malaria is the leading cause of mortality among children in Africa and costs the continent around $12 billion in lost productivity each year.
workedExamples.answer: The one-death-every-30-seconds figure checks out; mortality peaks among African children, with about $12 billion lost per year.

commonMistakes: Using pandemic and epidemic interchangeably; a pandemic officially exists only when an epidemic crosses a country's borders.
Believing COVID-19 began as the first recorded pandemic; the Great Plague of Athens in 430 BC is the first recorded pandemic.
Assuming the Spanish Flu started in Spain; it was first observed in Europe, the United States and parts of Asia, and Madrid's news reports only gave it the name.
Thinking health spending is fairly distributed; only 12 percent of 2002's $3.2 trillion reached nations with 90 percent of the illness burden.
Dating Ebola to later years; its index case was reported in December 2013 in Guinea.
Believing health crises affect all countries equally; impoverished countries always suffer more than developed ones.
applications: Connecting Ethiopia's 1918 Great Ethiopian Influenza (Ye Hedar Beshita) to the global Spanish Flu as a local case of a world pandemic.
Mapping how AIDS was first observed in America, Ebola in West Africa and COVID-19 in China's Hubei Province to compare outbreak geography.
Explaining why guidance from the Ebola experience, minimum capacity to detect, report and respond quickly, matters for Ethiopia's health system planning.
Calculating the gap between Africa's malaria burden and global health financing to argue for partnerships like the Global Fund.
Discussing the socio-economic effects of COVID-19 school closures and job losses on households that already pay out of pocket for care.
g12-geography-ug5-t5.summary: About 2 billion people lack basic health services, and global financing is deeply unequal: nations bearing 90 percent of the illness burden receive only a small share of world health spending, while malaria alone kills more than a million yearly at a cost of $12 billion to Africa. Pandemics have run from the Great Plague of Athens in 430 BC through the 1918 Spanish Flu, remembered in Ethiopia as Ye Hedar Beshita, to today's HIV/AIDS, Ebola and COVID-19. Poverty and weak governance mean poor countries always suffer more from health crises than developed ones.

events.text: Agrarian settlement 10,000 years ago - malaria, tuberculosis, leprosy, smallpox appear
Great Plague of Athens during the Peloponnesian War - two-thirds may have died
Spanish Flu pandemic - 50 million deaths worldwide; Ye Hedar Beshita in Ethiopia
AIDS first identified - first observed in America
WHO pivot: aid rises after creation of the Global Fund and vaccine alliance
Ebola index patient, a boy in Guinea - 11,310 deaths in three West African states
COVID-19 declared a pandemic; 75 million cases by December 2020

questions.q: Globally, approximately how many people do not have access to basic health services?
questions.explanation: The textbook estimates 2 billion individuals lack access to basic health services.

questions.q: Malaria causes approximately one death every 30 seconds worldwide.
questions.explanation: The text equates malaria's more than one million yearly deaths with one death every 30 seconds.

questions.q: How much of the $3.2 trillion spent on health care worldwide in 2002 went to low- and middle-income nations?
questions.answer: 12 percent
questions.explanation: Only 12 percent was spent in low- and middle-income nations, which hold 90 percent of the illness burden.

questions.q: A disease officially becomes a pandemic when:
options: it kills more than one million people
an epidemic spreads beyond a country's borders
questions.explanation: When an epidemic spreads beyond a country's borders, the disease officially becomes a pandemic.

questions.q: Explain the possible role of the Great Plague of Athens in the Peloponnesian War.
questions.answer: it weakened the Athenians significantly and was a significant factor in their defeat
questions.explanation: The suspected typhoid fever significantly weakened Athens and was a significant factor in its defeat by the Spartans.

questions.q: The epidemic that passed through Libya, Ethiopia and Egypt before entering Athens is known as what?
questions.answer: the Great Plague of Athens
questions.explanation: The Great Plague of Athens of 430 BC passed through Libya, Ethiopia and Egypt before crossing the Athenian walls.

questions.q: AIDS was first observed in Africa.
questions.explanation: The textbook states AIDS was first observed in America, though first identified in 1981.

questions.q: Why did Ebola hit Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone so hard? Give at least two reasons from the text.
questions.answer: vulnerable public health infrastructure|aftermath of civil war|lack of basic sanitation|no minimum core capacity to detect, report and respond
questions.explanation: These states had historically weak health systems, devastated by civil war, poor sanitation and lacking core outbreak response capacity.

questions.q: On what date did the WHO declare COVID-19 a pandemic, and how many cases and countries had been reached?
questions.answer: March 11, 2020|118,000 cases in 114 nations
questions.explanation: The declaration came after the virus infected over 118,000 individuals in 114 nations in three months.

questions.q: By December 2020, COVID-19 had:
options: infected more than 75 million people and killed more than 1.6 million
been controlled by a vaccine launched in 2020
infected fewer than one million people
questions.explanation: By December 2020, more than 75 million people were infected and more than 1.6 million had died.

questions.q: Arrange these events in chronological order.
options: Ebola index patient reported in Guinea
COVID-19 first reported case in Hubei, China
questions.explanation: The order is Spanish Flu (1918), AIDS identified (1981), Ebola index case (December 2013), COVID-19 first case (November 17, 2019).
